#339. Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

For children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world. With movies like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, The Land Before Time, All Dogs Go to Heaven, and Anastasia, this American animator offered us realms of adventure, with plucky heroes as well as villains so fantastically frightening that we carry the thrill of it all with us decades later.

Social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs. Brisby being chased down by monstrous, roaring, ravenous cats. Now, for fans new and old, filmmakers Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker offer Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, a documentary that explores the life and work of the innovative animator through his own words.

In an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues. Together, they pursued animation not for the money but for the art and a deep desire to create something meaningful for future generations. Yet, when asked about his legacy, Bluth is quick to look back on the path that led him to his work.

He began by speaking of Winsor McCay, the father of American animation. In a wistful storyteller tone, Bluth recounted how a little boy witnessed the "magic" of the 1914 short film Gertie the Dinosaur, in which a pencil-sketched brontosaurus comes to life. This little boy was so inspired that he'd grow up to make his own animated short featuring a mouse named Mickey.

That little boy, of course, was Walt Disney, who would go on to make 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first animated feature film produced in the United States. That movie would go on to inspire a young Bluth, who'd direct his first animated feature in 1982 with The Secret of NIMH.

This path of inspiration to iconic art wasn't as direct a line as you might think.

Yes, Bluth scored a dream job, working at Disney Animation studio for 10 years on films like Sleeping Beauty, Robin Hood, and The Rescuers. But after Disney's death in 1966, Bluth and 17 other Disney animators feared the studio had lost their way, creatively.

He told Mashable he'd invite these artists to his home on weekends, where they'd draw together to develop innovative pitches for their corporate bosses. When they were shot down, Bluth — along with Gary Goldman and John Pomeroy — built their own company, Don Bluth Productions, to "see if we could do better than they were doing." For this, Bluth remembered, "We were called traitors."

That's not how Bluth saw his team. "[These] wonderful people had the courage to leave their jobs and security and go out there and try and do something great," he said, "not just to feed their egos, but something they felt helped them grow up. And they wanted to give back."

It was not an easy journey, as Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There details, revealing the highs and lows of Bluth's most beloved and worst-reviewed productions, as well as the wildly popular video game Dragon's Lair. In our interview, he spoke repeatedly about how the doc filled him with gratitude as he looked back for the filmmakers' interviews.

To Mashable, he reflected, "What happened after so many movies, All Dogs Go to Heaven, American Tail, working with Steven Spielberg on both of those pictures, and George Lucas [on The Land Before Time], [it] became really, really obvious to us that we were doing the right thing [by] writing the right stories, and trying to make something that would move people's lives for the better — not just to pat our own backs and say, 'Look what we did.' [We were making] something that would help maybe children grow up and have some degree of morality about them. So then, that was our goal in everything."

In Somewhere Out There, the rise of computer animation — which Bluth refers to as "3D animation" — came as a devastating blow to the animator, who'd spent his life developing the skills of hand-drawn 2D animation. To this day, Bluth still advocates for the artistry of hand-drawn animation.

"The way I look at this is animation in the 2D form is people, armed with a pencil in their hands, have to be able to draw," he explained, "and they also have to be able to act. And they have to have feelings about story."

To Bluth, CGI movies aren't animation. "3D animation is puppetry," he said, adding, "[With 3D animation,] you drop your pencil. You put your hands on a keyboard, and you make a wireframe puppet act."

Bluth shared several of his complaints about the look of 3D animation, saying, "To me, it looks very plastic... The colors are muted, and they're trying to put shading in there, trying to look more like a live-action picture." He asked, "Why are we trying to get to a place which looks more real?" adding, "That isn't the purpose at all of 2D [animation]. The purpose is to take you to a magical world. 2D is trying to make audiences come to our own world."

Noting the animation industry changed forever with the massive success of 1995's Toy Story, Bluth said, "Toy Story [movies] were quite fun to watch, but they didn't make me feel anything very deep. And animation is intended to do that, particularly with Walt Disney pictures. Snow White, Bambi, [and] Pinocchio — those pictures did something to change the way you thought and help you grow up in a way that was really good. And they did it in such a beautiful way."

It was when Disney Studios, post-Walt, moved away from these tenets that Bluth and his colleagues set out on their own. He said, "We left the Disney Studio because it was leaving out the morality statements and leaving out all the beautiful colors and everything."

In terms of what recent animated films impressed Bluth, he said, "I liked Klaus a lot," commending Sergio Pablos' inventive Christmas tale, which employs hand-drawn animation with a unique visual style.

Bluth also enjoyed Pete Docter's 2009 Pixar hit Up. "That was totally in 3D," he noted, "but it had a great story. For my taste, it went on too long. You know, the story was really about this couple promising each other they would go back to some place in their life, and she died. So, the man, true to the promise, tries to fulfill that [by taking their house on the journey]. So, I love that."

Overall though, Bluth lamented, "Animation has become an advertisement for sugar cereal and whatever. There are more advertisements on animation than there are actually animated characters. The animated characters are just simply little puppets that jump up and down and tell one-line jokes. So, that's not good. Now, the last laugh is about to hit us like a tsunami; that is AI."

Through the stories of Russian Jewish immigrant Fievel Mousekewitz, the widowed mother of four Mrs. Brisby, the orphaned brontosaurus Littlefoot, and rogue mutt Charlie B. Barkin, Bluth was striving to create stories that would inspire children to be good and creative, as Disney's movies had done for him. He doesn't see a future where AI can provide such mindful, moral guidance.

"It seems like AI is able to do wonderful, wonderful things," Bluth mused, "except AI is a machine, and it has no soul. It will borrow or steal, if you will, from everything that it knows, and give you what you ask for. But where's the creativity?"

"AI is a borrower," Bluth explained. "When you enter what you'd like to see, it searches all over and borrows it from other artists, puts it together. It shows you on screen. Now, you can then make corrections. It can do all that, but it is still a machine. It doesn't ask you, 'Well, what is right and wrong? What is evil and good? What do you want me to say?' The machine can't do that."

He continued, "The only thing you can do is go back to human beings and say, 'Don't replace human beings with machines.' They're the ones who have a heart, who have a soul, and probably have a Creator. So, there's a bigger picture that's going on than just animation on a screen."

"AI has no soul," Bluth concluded. "It hasn't a clue how to write anything. Everything that you're going to see on your screen has been stolen from other artists."

He allowed that some AI might be "stunningly beautiful," but "you'll find that it doesn't affect your heart the way you feel… They're not artists that are doing the AI. Many of them don't understand the art of acting or anything. So, what everything looks like in AI animation that I've seen, it all looks like slow motion, and it looks unreal. So, that's definitely a road I don't want to travel on."

"I read somewhere where someone said something that stuck in my head," he mused, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde's The Portrait of Dorian Gray. "There are many people who know the price of everything but the value of nothing. And I certainly hope that's not where we're going."

#338. The Best Pura Deals for Cyber Week (2026)

Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser. Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work by blowing air through oil) for years due to its ease of use and sprawling library of high-end scents.

In fact, no brand even comes close to Pura's sheer breadth of available fragrances—with more than 150 options from big names like Anthropologie, Nest, LAFCO, Brooklyn Candle Company, Studio McGee, and more. Pura even has special seasonal collabs, like this month’s Nutcracker-inspired scents from the New York City Ballet. These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).

But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo. (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.)

Cartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.

Pura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (though I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no issues in six months of testing.

If you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the new Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.

I also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.

There’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale (MSRP averages $21 apiece, and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.

Also on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar, which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.

Another Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces, which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). However, it did do a great job of scenting a high-ceilinged room on the first floor of my house.

#337. Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

TP-Link’s struggle illustrates how Trump admin wields control over device makers.

TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link says.

TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any new technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie said in a joint statement.

The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

The US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

For the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, new additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List currently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

“The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”

McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

“The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”

Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre said the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

McIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any company receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she said.

TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft said in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

Security expert Bruce Schneier said there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier said.

With routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”

When asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese company, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”

TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier said that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”

TP-Link says the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article said, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”

TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the company doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, said in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

“TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he said. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese company. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”

TP-Link said in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”

In 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

TP-Link’s response to Joyce said it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The company says in a fact sheet that when routers provided to users by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”

Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”

Last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

“Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the company’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

“Any time a company has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” said Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

Marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a company has larger issues pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he said.

Although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a company official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he said.

“There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he said. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”

Kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the company’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

Kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”

Kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the company’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he said. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”

Kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he said. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”

Kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”

Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency plans if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”

Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not currently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”

Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she said others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring plans.

“I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she said.

The FCC said the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”

Although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

After the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre said.

Under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

“We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC said in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”

The FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

“The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill says.

The CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement said the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”

#336. iOS 27.3 Apple Intelligence, Siri AI usage limits: What to know

All good things must come to an end implement usage limits.

Just a few months after Apple finally launched the long-awaited Siri AI, its upgraded voice assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, the company will now implement daily usage limits. These new restrictions will be implemented along with the launch of iOS 27.3.

What does this mean? Basically, if a user hits those limits, they will need to upgrade their paid iCloud+ account or wait for the daily limits to reset. However, not every Siri AI request counts towards users' daily limits.

So, what counts towards your daily Siri AI limits? How much does it cost to upgrade? Lets break down everything you need to know about the new Siri AI usage limits.

According to Apple, "Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for users with a supported device set to a supported language." However, "some features rely on powerful server models and have limits."

Apple says the following features will have daily usage limits:

Images: Intelligent Photo Editing Tools, which include Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, as well as Image Playground

Workflows and automation: AFM Cloud and AFM Cloud Pro models in Shortcuts

Third-party apps that use Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

Apple has not published exactly what the daily usage limits are for Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. The company's Support page simply describes it as a "generous daily usage limit."

Notably, each of those above categories has its own unique daily usage limits. These are not shared between those features, which means a user can hit the daily limit for one but not the others.

Daily usage limits are connected at the Apple account level and are implemented across all Apple devices, including iOS devices, Mac, and Apple TV.

When a user reaches their daily limit, they will receive a prompt after making a request that counts towards those limits. Advanced requests are paused until the daily limit resets or the user upgrades to an iCloud+ plan.

"Daily Request Limit Reached," the prompt reads on iOS. "You can continue with basic requests."

The prompt also includes a button to upgrade to an iCloud+ plan to increase those daily limits.

As previously mentioned, Apple isn't sharing exactly what those Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits are. However, they have shared just how many times those "generous" limits are increased when upgrading to an iCloud+ plan.

Here's an outline of what you get with each iCloud+ plan: The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

200GB: $2.99 per month – Up to 2x daily usage limit

2TB: $9.99 per month – Up to 5x daily usage limit

6TB: $29.99 per month – Up to 10x daily usage limit

12TB: $59.99 per month – Up to 20x daily usage limit

The 50GB iCloud+ plan, which Apple sells for $0.99 per month, does not include any increase in daily usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

Apple says that all feature categories will have their daily limits reset at approximately midnight in the user's current time zone.

According to Apple, users who are travelling internationally will have their limits reset "around midnight in the central time zone of the country or region of your Apple Account." Users who share an iCloud+ plan with a Family Sharing group will see their limits reset at around midnight of the time zone of the iCloud+ plan purchaser. Users who aren't signed into their Apple Account will see their limits reset around 24 hours after they first used that feature category that day.

Unused limits from the previous day do not roll over.

Starting with iOS 27.3, Siri AI will also receive limits for certain "advanced" tasks. Apple says that basic tasks will continue to be unlimited and will work even when the daily usage limits for advanced tasks are reached.

You may be wondering what a "basic" task is and what is an "advanced" task, the latter of which will have daily usage limits.

Apple provided the following examples as a basic task, which users will be able to utilize without limits:

"Text Mark that Annika's party is at 123 Main Street.”

As for advanced tasks, Apple provides these examples:

"Text Mark the address for Annika's party, and tell him what time we need to leave from home to make it on time."

"Add a summary of my San Francisco trip note to this email draft."

Based on those examples, it appears advanced tasks involve multi-step requests that require server-side processing.

Beyond Apple's official published examples, Apple leaker pdfu has uncovered Apple's more detailed instructions given to Siri AI telling the assistant how to decide if a user has reached their limits for advanced tasks. In an X post, the leaker explained Siri will take limits into account if a user request:

uses information from one app, from what is on screen or from a message, in a different app, or needs a result from one step used in a different step or app (such as a looked-up fact typed into a field)

contains two or more separate asks in one sentence, even in the same app (extra details of one action, such as a cc or a time, are still one ask)

asks about or summarizes the content of a photo, a camera view or an attachment (editing, searching and albums are fine)

deletes, archives, junks, moves, marks or changes a set (all, every, these or a whole category) of the user’s emails, notes, reminders, messages, photos, files, contacts or events

sets a device action or a notification to run on a time or trigger (not alarms, timers, reminders or calendar events), notifies someone when a person arrives or leaves, or builds or edits a Shortcut or automation

is deep research or a multi-step task done on the user’s behalf

asks you to compose or create new content (a story, poem, essay, plan, recipe, image, or an email or message from a topic rather than wording the user gives), or to rewrite in a tone other than friendly, professional or concise

A user asking a third-party AI assistant like ChatGPT for an advanced request is never limited, even if a user reaches their daily usage limit for the day.

According to pdfu, tasks like "proofreading, rewriting in a friendly, professional or concise tone, summaries as key points, a list or a table, typing or sending wording the user gives, a single direct operation in any app, even when Siri must look the target up first (the closest bakery, my cousin), 'this' or 'that' within its own app, running a Shortcut by name, a reminder for yourself by time or place, Find My, sharing your ETA or location, and all your home accessories (lights, doors, locks), alarms, timers or device settings" all fall under basic tasks.

So far, Apple hasn't released much more on these new daily usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. Hopefully, before iOS 27.3 comes out, Apple provides users with more specific information regarding what does and doesn't count towards their daily usage limits.

#332. Don’t Bring Jensen Back

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.

Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.

Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.

It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?

The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.

At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.

Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.

The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?)

There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.

On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”

Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.

Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

#331. Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend

World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

#330. Anthropic claims Claude solved 2 enduring mysteries about black holes

At a time when Anthropic is vacuuming up stock market money, the AI company has made a pretty grandiose claim about its Claude chatbot's scientific capabilities.

The San Francisco-based artificial intelligence firm published a lengthy blog post this week claiming that its Claude Fable 5.2 model had made some progress on figuring out two long-standing mysteries surrounding black holes. The post goes into an incredible amount of scientific detail that might fly over your head (as much of it did mine), but I'll try my best to summarize it in plain English.

According to Anthropic, the first conundrum Claude was able to solve involved the concept of heating up a hypothetical universe. When the universe reaches a certain temperature, it would form a black hole through a sudden "phase transition," as initially described by Stephen Hawking and Don Page in 1983. Hawking and Page's findings concerned only a vast universe described by general relativity, while this theoretical universe is much smaller and might work differently.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

It turns out, as Claude found, that the phase transition is also abrupt in a smaller universe. As Anthropic explained, this implies that "black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory."

As for the second finding, it revolves around another theoretical universe made up of two dimensions instead of three. In this universe, physicists have spent years trying to figure out how heavy the lightest possible black hole could be using a technique called "bootstrapping," in which the ceiling for the lightest black hole gets lowered each time a theory breaks it. Anthropic claimed that Claude Fable 5.2 was able to notice a pattern that physicists had missed in their calculations and use it to "calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered."

As Anthropic was quick to point out in the blog post, these findings do not apply to our universe or have any practical application but could give us an idea of how relativity and quantum mechanics work together. It's also worth noting that these findings were released alongside Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO, AKA a time when Anthropic wants as much public money as possible.

#329. Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way

Your support for Ars matters more now than ever.

It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

But I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

Since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re important. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an important backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

Focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s new in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the big questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

But I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

One reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

The former is important because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

All of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

But it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

It’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

We’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#325. Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”

Neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings says that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”

Multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

The Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

As of 2026, DraftKings launched “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

“Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

“Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”

In June 2026, DraftKings launched what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”

Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

“Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#323. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#321. Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI

Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.

Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.

The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

#320. Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing

Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.

Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”

The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI.

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.)

Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”

Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.
